title: Medical Virology and Mycology
description: Structure, replication and laboratory diagnosis of medically important viruses and fungi, including viral haemorrhagic fevers, hepatitis viruses, HIV and fungal infections common in Nigeria.

topics.title: General Virology and Laboratory Methods
topics.summary: Virus structure, classification, replication and diagnostic approaches.

notes.b: Viruses are obligate intracellular parasites containing either DNA or RNA (never both) within a protein capsid (icosahedral or helical symmetry), sometimes surrounded by a lipid envelope derived from host membranes (enveloped viruses are sensitive to detergents, drying and ether; non-enveloped viruses such as poliovirus, rotavirus and norovirus are more resistant). The Baltimore classification groups viruses by genome type and replication strategy (e.g. dsDNA — herpesviruses; +ssRNA — polio, hepatitis C, flaviviruses, coronaviruses; −ssRNA — influenza, measles, rabies, Lassa (ambisense arenavirus), Ebola; retroviruses — HIV with reverse transcriptase; hepadnaviruses — HBV, a partially double-stranded DNA virus replicating via RNA). Replication steps: attachment, penetration, uncoating, synthesis of components, assembly and release (budding or lysis). Antivirals target these steps.

Laboratory diagnosis of viral infections: direct detection — nucleic acid amplification (PCR, RT-PCR — the mainstay), antigen detection (ELISA, rapid tests — e.g. HBsAg, rotavirus, influenza, dengue NS1), electron microscopy (rarely); virus isolation in cell culture (cytopathic effect, e.g. syncytia with RSV and measles; haemadsorption with influenza) — slow and needs containment; and serology — IgM (recent infection), IgG seroconversion or fourfold titre rise, IgG avidity. Specimens depend on the virus: nasopharyngeal swabs in viral transport medium (respiratory viruses), stool (enteroviruses, rotavirus), blood/plasma (HIV, hepatitis, VHFs), CSF, vesicle fluid (herpesviruses, mpox), and urine; keep cold (4 °C) and transport quickly; freeze at −70 °C for longer storage.

topics.title: Viral Haemorrhagic Fevers and Arboviruses
topics.summary: Lassa fever, Ebola, yellow fever, dengue, and laboratory safety for high-consequence pathogens.

notes.b: Lassa fever, first described in Lassa, Borno State (1969), is caused by an arenavirus (bisegmented ambisense RNA) carried by the multimammate rat Mastomys natalensis; humans are infected through contact with rodent excreta or contaminated food and person-to-person via body fluids (nosocomial outbreaks). Nigeria reports thousands of suspected cases annually (peak December–April), with case fatality around 15–20% among confirmed cases. Diagnosis: RT-PCR on blood in BSL-3/4-capable laboratories (Irrua Specialist Teaching Hospital, NCDC National Reference Laboratory, Lagos University Teaching Hospital, FMC Owo, ACEGID); early ribavirin improves survival. Ebola virus disease (filovirus) — Nigeria contained its 2014 importation (Patrick Sawyer case) through aggressive contact tracing; diagnosis by RT-PCR (GeneXpert Ebola). Laboratory staff must use full PPE and inactivate samples before routine testing; minimise non-essential tests.

Arboviruses are transmitted by arthropods. Yellow fever (flavivirus; Aedes and Haemagogus mosquitoes; sylvatic and urban cycles) causes fever, jaundice, haemorrhage and renal failure; recurrent Nigerian outbreaks (2017–2023) drive vaccination campaigns; a single dose of 17D live vaccine gives lifelong protection. Diagnosis: IgM ELISA (cross-reacts with other flaviviruses — confirm by plaque reduction neutralisation test at reference labs such as the Institut Pasteur Dakar) and RT-PCR early. Dengue (four serotypes; Aedes aegypti) — NS1 antigen in the first days, IgM later; secondary infection with a different serotype risks severe dengue (antibody-dependent enhancement); dengue is under-recognised in Nigeria because febrile illness is presumed to be malaria. Others: chikungunya, Zika (microcephaly), West Nile, and Crimean–Congo haemorrhagic fever (ticks).

topics.title: Hepatitis Viruses and HIV
topics.summary: Hepatitis A–E, HBV and HCV markers and load, HIV testing and monitoring.

notes.b: Hepatitis A (picornavirus) and E (hepevirus) are faeco-orally transmitted and cause acute infection (HEV is dangerous in pregnancy — high mortality); diagnosis by IgM antibodies. Hepatitis B (hepadnavirus) prevalence in Nigeria is about 8–10% — highly endemic; transmission is mother-to-child, sexual, blood and horizontal in childhood; chronic infection risks cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma. Markers: HBsAg (infection), anti-HBs (immunity), anti-HBc IgM (acute) and total (exposure), HBeAg (high replication), HBV DNA (viral load — guides treatment with tenofovir and prevention of mother-to-child transmission). Hepatitis D (delta) needs HBV (defective virus) — co-infection or superinfection causes severe disease. Hepatitis C (flavivirus; prevalence about 1–2%) — blood-borne; anti-HCV screening then HCV RNA; cured by direct-acting antivirals (sofosbuvir-based) in 8–12 weeks; genotyping less needed with pangenotypic regimens.
k: HAV and HEV: faeco-oral; HEV severe in pregnancy
HCV: anti-HCV then RNA; DAAs cure

notes.b: HIV-1 (predominant; several subtypes, CRF02_AG common in Nigeria) and HIV-2 (West Africa, less pathogenic) are retroviruses. Diagnosis: serial rapid test algorithm (Determine → Unigold → tie-breaker), fourth-generation antigen/antibody ELISA; infants under 18 months need nucleic acid testing (DNA PCR from dried blood spots at 6 weeks) because maternal antibodies persist. Monitoring: HIV viral load (RT-PCR — the key indicator of treatment success; suppression < 1,000 copies/mL, ideally < 50), CD4 count by flow cytometry (baseline to detect advanced disease, cryptococcal antigen screening if CD4 < 200), and drug resistance testing (genotyping by sequencing the pol gene) for treatment failure. Recency assays distinguish recent from long-standing infection for surveillance. The window period is reduced by fourth-generation tests and NAT.

topics.title: Other Important Viral Infections
topics.summary: Respiratory viruses, measles, polio, rabies, herpesviruses, HPV and mpox.

notes.b: Influenza (orthomyxovirus; segmented genome — antigenic drift causes seasonal epidemics, antigenic shift causes pandemics; haemagglutinin and neuraminidase), respiratory syncytial virus (bronchiolitis in infants), and SARS-CoV-2 (coronavirus — RT-PCR and antigen tests) are diagnosed on respiratory samples. Measles (paramyxovirus) — fever, cough, coryza, conjunctivitis, Koplik spots and rash; complications include pneumonia, encephalitis and malnutrition; diagnosis by IgM ELISA on serum (case-based surveillance). Poliovirus (enterovirus) — acute flaccid paralysis surveillance collects two stool samples 24–48 hours apart within 14 days of onset for culture at WHO-accredited labs (Ibadan and Maiduguri); environmental surveillance of sewage detects circulation; cVDPV2 is controlled with nOPV2. Rabies (lyssavirus; dog bites) is almost 100% fatal once symptomatic; post-mortem diagnosis by fluorescent antibody test on brain tissue (Negri bodies histologically); prevention with wound washing, vaccine and immunoglobulin.
k: Rabies: FAT on brain; Negri bodies

notes.b: Herpesviruses establish latency: HSV-1 and HSV-2 (oral and genital ulcers, encephalitis — CSF PCR), varicella-zoster virus (chickenpox and shingles), cytomegalovirus (congenital infection, disease in immunocompromised — CMV viral load), Epstein–Barr virus (infectious mononucleosis; associated with Burkitt lymphoma and nasopharyngeal carcinoma), HHV-8 (Kaposi sarcoma). Human papillomavirus causes warts (types 6, 11) and cervical, anal and oropharyngeal cancers (types 16, 18) — HPV DNA testing for screening. Mpox (orthopoxvirus) re-emerged in Nigeria in 2017 (clade IIb, with sustained human transmission); vesicular/pustular lesions with lymphadenopathy; diagnosis by PCR on lesion swabs (roof or fluid of vesicles, or crusts). Viral gastroenteritis in children is mainly rotavirus (antigen test; vaccine introduced in Nigeria in 2022) and norovirus.

topics.title: Medical Mycology
topics.summary: Superficial, subcutaneous and systemic mycoses, opportunistic fungi and laboratory diagnosis.

notes.b: Fungi are eukaryotes with chitin cell walls and ergosterol membranes; they exist as yeasts, moulds (hyphae) or dimorphic forms (mould at 25 °C, yeast at 37 °C). Superficial mycoses: pityriasis versicolor (Malassezia — 'spaghetti and meatballs' on KOH), dermatophytoses (Trichophyton, Microsporum, Epidermophyton — tinea capitis is common in Nigerian schoolchildren, tinea corporis, pedis, cruris; Wood's lamp fluorescence for some Microsporum). Subcutaneous mycoses (traumatic implantation, common in rural tropical areas): mycetoma (Madura foot — eumycetoma caused by fungi, e.g. Madurella mycetomatis, versus actinomycetoma by bacteria; grains of different colours; common in northern Nigeria), chromoblastomycosis (sclerotic 'copper penny' bodies) and sporotrichosis. Laboratory methods: KOH (10–20%) wet mounts, calcofluor white, culture on Sabouraud dextrose agar (with chloramphenicol and cycloheximide) at 25–30 °C for up to 4 weeks, and lactophenol cotton blue mounts for identification.

Opportunistic fungi affect immunocompromised patients (HIV, diabetes, chemotherapy, steroids, ICU). Candida albicans causes oral thrush, vulvovaginal candidiasis, oesophagitis (AIDS-defining) and candidaemia; germ tube test (positive in 2–3 hours in serum) and chromogenic agars identify species; Candida auris is a multidrug-resistant emerging threat. Cryptococcus neoformans causes meningitis in advanced HIV — India ink shows capsules in CSF; cryptococcal antigen (CrAg) lateral flow assay on serum or CSF is highly sensitive. Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP — silver or immunofluorescence stains; cotrimoxazole prophylaxis). Aspergillus (acute-angle branching septate hyphae; aspergilloma in old TB cavities — common after TB in Nigeria; galactomannan antigen). Mucorales (broad, ribbon-like aseptate hyphae with right-angle branching — rhinocerebral mucormycosis in diabetic ketoacidosis). Histoplasma capsulatum var. duboisii (African histoplasmosis — large yeasts in skin and bone lesions). Antifungals: azoles (fluconazole), amphotericin B, flucytosine, echinocandins.
